p.src: The story tells how Tripitaka, obeying the Bodhisattva's instructions, took the Pilgrim back. Together with Bajie and Sha Monk, they cast aside their divided minds, reined in the ape and horse, and pressed toward the Western Heaven with united hearts and strength. There is no telling how swiftly time flew, like an arrow, while the days and months sped like a shuttle. They passed through the scorching months of summer, and soon the frosty scenes of autumn arrived. There they saw:

p.src: As the master and his three disciples journeyed onward, they gradually felt a stifling heat rising around them. Tripitaka reined in his horse and said, “It is autumn now, so why has the weather turned hot again?” Bajie said, “You do not know the reason. On the road west lies the kingdom of Sihali, where the sun sets, commonly called the end of the sky. Toward the hours of the Monkey and Rooster, the king sends men onto the city walls to beat drums and blow horns, mingling their din with the boiling roar of the sea. The sun is true solar fire; when it sinks into the Western Sea, it is like red-hot fire plunged into water, and the meeting makes the sea boil with a tremendous noise. If the drums and horns did not confuse the ear, that thunderous sound would shake every child in the city to death. Since the heat here is so oppressive, we must be nearing the place where the sun sets.” Hearing this, the Great Sage could not help laughing. “Stop talking nonsense, idiot. As for the kingdom of Sihali, it is still far too early to speak of reaching it. If Master keeps delaying as he does, wavering from one day to the next, we could pass from childhood to old age, grow young and old through three lifetimes, and still never arrive.” Bajie said, “Brother! If, as you say, this is not where the sun sets, why is it so unbearably hot?” Sha Monk said, “Perhaps the seasons are out of joint, and summer weather is prevailing in autumn.” While the three of them were arguing, they saw an estate beside the road: its houses were roofed with red tiles, its walls built of red bricks, its doors coated in red oil, and its benches painted with red lacquer. Everything was red. Tripitaka dismounted and said, “Wukong, go to that house and ask what is happening here and why it is so hot.”

p.src: The Great Sage put away his gold-banded cudgel, straightened his clothes, and affected the refined manner of a gentleman. Stepping off the main road, he went directly to the gate and looked around. Suddenly an old man came out through the gate. This was his appearance:

p.src: The old man suddenly looked up and, seeing the Pilgrim, started in fright. Leaning on his bamboo staff, he shouted, “Where have you come from, you monster? What business have you at my gate?” The Pilgrim returned his greeting and said, “Do not be afraid of me, venerable patron. I am no monster. This poor monk is an imperial envoy from the Great Tang in the Eastern Land, bound for the West to seek the scriptures. Our party of master and three disciples has just arrived in your worthy district. We neither understand why the weather is so oppressively hot nor know the name of this place, so I have come especially to ask you to enlighten us.” Only then did the old man relax, and he smiled. “Please forgive me, Reverend. My old eyes blurred for a moment, and I failed to recognize your honored countenance.” “Not at all,” said the Pilgrim. The old man then asked, “On which road is your master?” The Pilgrim said, “Is that not he standing on the main road to the south?” The old man said, “Please invite him in, please invite him in.” Delighted, the Pilgrim beckoned. Tripitaka came forward with Bajie and Sha Monk, leading the white horse and carrying the luggage, and they all bowed to the old man.

p.src: When the old man saw Tripitaka's handsome and dignified bearing and the strange, extraordinary looks of Bajie and Sha Monk, he was both startled and delighted. He invited them inside to sit, ordered his servants to serve tea, and had a meal prepared at the same time. Hearing this, Tripitaka rose to thank him and said, “May I ask, venerable sir, why your worthy district turns so hot when autumn arrives?” The old man replied, “This place is called the Mountain of Flames. It has neither spring nor autumn, and is hot in all four seasons.” Tripitaka asked, “In which direction does the Mountain of Flames lie? Does it block the road west?” The old man said, “You cannot go west. The mountain lies sixty li from here, directly across the only road west. Its flames extend for eight hundred li, and not a blade of grass grows anywhere around it. If anyone tried to cross it, even with a bronze skull and an iron body, he would melt into liquid.” At these words Tripitaka turned pale with alarm and dared ask no more.

p.src: Just then a young man appeared outside the gate, pushing a little red cart. He stopped beside the gate and called, “Cakes for sale!” The Great Sage plucked a hair, changed it into a copper coin, and asked the man to sell him a cake. The man took the coin without examining it, lifted the cloth covering the cart, and amid billowing steam took out a cake and handed it to the Pilgrim. In the Pilgrim's hand it felt like a burning coal from the fire or a red-hot nail from a brazier. Look at him tossing it from his left hand to his right and back again, crying, “Hot, hot, hot! Impossible to eat, impossible to eat!” The young man laughed. “If you fear the heat, do not come here. This place is always this hot.” The Pilgrim said, “You fellow, you make no sense. As the proverb says, ‘If it is neither cold nor hot, the five grains will not ripen.’ But when it is as fiercely hot as this, where does the flour for your cakes come from?” The man replied, “If you would know where the rice for the cake flour comes from, respectfully seek the Iron-Fan Immortal.” The Pilgrim asked, “What has the Iron-Fan Immortal to do with it?” The man said, “The Iron-Fan Immortal possesses a plantain-leaf fan. If we can obtain it, the first wave extinguishes the fire, the second raises a wind, and the third brings rain. Then we sow our fields and reap the harvest in season, and thus obtain the five grains that sustain our lives; otherwise, truly not a single blade of grass could grow.”

p.src: Hearing this, the Pilgrim hurried back inside and handed the cake to Tripitaka. “Do not worry, Master, and do not fret a year in advance. Eat this cake, and I shall explain.” The elder took the cake and said to the old master of the house, “Venerable sir, please have some cake.” The old man said, “I have not yet served you the tea and meal from my own house. How could I presume to eat your cake?” The Pilgrim laughed. “There is no need to trouble yourself with tea or food, venerable sir. Let me ask you: where does the Iron-Fan Immortal live?” The old man asked, “Why do you seek her?” The Pilgrim said, “The cake seller just told me that this immortal possesses a plantain-leaf fan. If it can be obtained, the first wave extinguishes the fire, the second raises a wind, and the third brings rain; only then can you sow and reap in this district and obtain the five grains that sustain life. I intend to find her and borrow it, so that I may fan out the Mountain of Flames and pass through, while also enabling the people here to sow and harvest in season and live in peace.” The old man said, “That is indeed so, but you have no gifts, and I fear the holy immortal will refuse to come.” Tripitaka asked, “What gifts does she require?” The old man replied, “The families here go to make supplication once every ten years. We take four pigs and four sheep, bolts of festive silk for inner and outer robes, rare incense, seasonal fruit, chickens, geese, and fine wine. After bathing and purifying ourselves, we devoutly worship at the immortal mountain, invite her out of her cave, and bring her here to exercise her power.” The Pilgrim asked, “Where is that mountain situated? What is the place called? How many li away is it? I shall go and ask her for the fan.” The old man replied, “The mountain lies to the southwest and is called Mount Green Cloud. On it is an immortal cave called Plantain Cave. When the faithful people from here go to worship at the immortal mountain, the round trip takes a month. The distance is some fourteen hundred and fifty or sixty li.” The Pilgrim laughed. “That is no trouble. I shall be back in no time.” The old man said, “Wait a while. Have some tea and food, prepare provisions for the road, and be sure to take two companions. There are no homes along the road, and many wolves and tigers. It cannot be reached in a single day, so do not treat this as a joke.” The Pilgrim laughed. “No need, no need. I am off.” With those words, he suddenly vanished. The old man cried in alarm, “Merciful heavens! So he is a divine being who rides the clouds and mist!”

p.src: The Pilgrim approached, bowed, and said, “Greetings, brother woodcutter.” The woodcutter put down his axe, returned the greeting, and asked, “Where are you bound, venerable sir?” The Pilgrim said, “May I ask, brother woodcutter, whether this is Mount Emerald Cloud?” “It is,” said the woodcutter. The Pilgrim asked, “Where is the Plantain Cave belonging to the Iron-Fan Immortal?” The woodcutter laughed. “There is indeed a Plantain Cave, but no Iron-Fan Immortal. There is only Princess Iron Fan, who is also called the Rakshasa Woman.” The Pilgrim said, “People say she has a plantain-leaf fan capable of extinguishing the flames of Fiery Mountain. Is that the woman?” “That is she, that is she,” said the woodcutter. “That worthy lady possesses this treasure, which is wonderfully able to quench the fire and protect the people of that region; hence she is called the Iron-Fan Immortal. We who live here have no need of her; we know her only as the Rakshasa Woman, wife of the mighty Bull Demon King.”

p.src: At these words the Pilgrim turned pale with shock and thought to himself, “Another enemy! Years ago, when I subdued Red Boy, they said he was this fellow’s son. Later, at Child-Destroying Cave on Mount Sun-Scorching, I met his uncle, who would not even give us water and meant to avenge him. Now that I have met his parents too, how shall I ever borrow this fan?” Seeing the Pilgrim sunk in silent thought and sighing without cease, the woodcutter laughed and said, “Venerable sir, you are a monk. What worries and doubts can you have? Follow this little path eastward for no more than five or six li and you will reach Plantain Cave. Do not fret.” The Pilgrim said, “To tell you the truth, brother woodcutter, I am the senior disciple of the Tang monk sent from the Great Tang in the Eastern Land to seek scriptures in the Western Heaven. The year before last, at Fire-Cloud Cave, I had a dispute with Red Boy, the Rakshasa Woman’s son. I fear she may bear a grudge and refuse me, and that is why I am troubled.” The woodcutter said, “A true man reads faces and judges moods. Say only that you have come to ask for the fan, and do not bring up that old nasty business. I warrant you will borrow it.” Hearing this, the Pilgrim bowed deeply and said, “Thank you for your instruction, brother woodcutter. I shall be off.”

p.src: The Pilgrim stepped forward and called, “Brother Bull, open the door! Open the door!” With a creak the cave door opened, and out came a serving girl, a flower basket in her hand and a hoe over her shoulder. Her clothes were truly ragged and without adornment, yet her face shone with vitality and the spirit of the Way. The Pilgrim met her with palms joined and said, “Young lady, may I trouble you to report to the princess that I am a scripture-seeking monk. Fiery Mountain blocks our westward road, so I have come especially to pay my respects and borrow the plantain-leaf fan for a while.” The serving girl asked, “From which monastery do you come? What is your name? Then I can announce you.” The Pilgrim replied, “I come from the Eastern Land, and I am the monk Sun Wukong.”

p.src: The Rakshasa Woman came out and shouted, “Where is Sun Wukong?” The Pilgrim stepped forward, bowed, and said, “Sister-in-law, Old Sun is here to pay his respects.” The Rakshasa Woman snapped, “Who is your sister-in-law? Who wants your respects?” The Pilgrim said, “Your honored husband, the Bull Demon King, once swore brotherhood with Old Sun. We were seven brothers bound as kin. Now that I hear the princess is Brother Bull’s honored wife, how could I not call you sister-in-law?” The Rakshasa Woman said, “You damned monkey! If you were bound to us as a brother, why did you bring ruin upon my son?” Feigning ignorance, the Pilgrim asked, “Who is your son?” The Rakshasa Woman said, “My son is Red Boy, the Sage Infant Great King of Fire-Cloud Cave in Withered-Pine Ravine on Mount Hao. You overthrew him, and we have had nowhere to seek you for vengeance. Now you have come to my door to offer up your life—do you think I shall spare you?” All smiles, the Pilgrim said, “Sister-in-law, you do not understand the truth of the matter and have wrongly blamed Old Sun. Your son seized my master and meant to steam and boil him. Fortunately, the Bodhisattva Guanyin took the boy away and rescued my master. He is now with the Bodhisattva as the Boy of Sudhana. He has truly attained the Bodhisattva’s righteous fruit: neither born nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, as long-lived as Heaven and Earth and as enduring as the sun and moon. Instead of thanking Old Sun for saving his life, you blame me. What reason is there in that?” The Rakshasa Woman said, “You glib-tongued, damned monkey! Even if my son was not killed, how can he return to my side? When shall I ever see him again?” The Pilgrim laughed. “Sister-in-law, if you wish to see your son, what difficulty is there? Just lend me the fan. Once I have fanned out the flames and escorted my master across, I shall go to the Bodhisattva in the Southern Sea and ask him to come see you. Then I shall return the fan. What objection could there be? Then you may see whether so much as a hair of him has been harmed. If he has suffered the slightest injury, you will have good cause to blame me. But if he is handsomer than before, you ought to thank me.” The Rakshasa Woman said, “Damned monkey! Enough of your prattle! Stretch out your head and let me hew at it a few times. If you can bear the pain, I shall lend you the fan. If you cannot endure it, I shall send you at once to meet King Yama.” The Pilgrim clasped his hands and stepped forward, laughing. “Sister-in-law, say no more. Old Sun will stretch out his bare head, and you may strike as many blows as you please. Stop only when your strength is spent. Only be sure to lend me the fan afterward.” Without allowing another word, the Rakshasa Woman brandished both swords and brought them clanging down on the Pilgrim’s head more than a dozen times, but the Pilgrim took no notice at all. The Rakshasa Woman took fright and turned to leave. The Pilgrim called, “Where are you going, sister-in-law? Hurry and lend it to me for a while.” The Rakshasa Woman replied, “My treasure is never lightly lent.” The Pilgrim said, “If you refuse to lend it, then taste a blow from your old uncle!”

You overthrew him, and we have had nowhere to seek you for vengeance. Now you have come to my door to offer up your life—do you think I shall spare you?”
All smiles, the Pilgrim said, “Sister-in-law, you do not understand the truth of the matter and have wrongly blamed Old Sun.
Your son seized my master and meant to steam and boil him. Fortunately, the Bodhisattva Guanyin took the boy away and rescued my master.

He is now with the Bodhisattva as the Boy of Sudhana. He has truly attained the Bodhisattva’s righteous fruit: neither born nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, as long-lived as Heaven and Earth and as enduring as the sun and moon.
Instead of thanking Old Sun for saving his life, you blame me. What reason is there in that?”
The Rakshasa Woman said, “You glib-tongued, damned monkey!
Even if my son was not killed, how can he return to my side? When shall I ever see him again?”
The Pilgrim laughed. “Sister-in-law, if you wish to see your son, what difficulty is there?

Just lend me the fan. Once I have fanned out the flames and escorted my master across, I shall go to the Bodhisattva in the Southern Sea and ask him to come see you. Then I shall return the fan. What objection could there be?
Then you may see whether so much as a hair of him has been harmed.
If he has suffered the slightest injury, you will have good cause to blame me.
But if he is handsomer than before, you ought to thank me.”
The Rakshasa Woman said, “Damned monkey!
Enough of your prattle! Stretch out your head and let me hew at it a few times. If you can bear the pain, I shall lend you the fan.
If you cannot endure it, I shall send you at once to meet King Yama.”
The Pilgrim clasped his hands and stepped forward, laughing. “Sister-in-law, say no more.
Old Sun will stretch out his bare head, and you may strike as many blows as you please. Stop only when your strength is spent.
Only be sure to lend me the fan afterward.”
Without allowing another word, the Rakshasa Woman brandished both swords and brought them clanging down on the Pilgrim’s head more than a dozen times, but the Pilgrim took no notice at all.
The Rakshasa Woman took fright and turned to leave.
The Pilgrim called, “Where are you going, sister-in-law?
Hurry and lend it to me for a while.”
The Rakshasa Woman replied, “My treasure is never lightly lent.”
The Pilgrim said, “If you refuse to lend it, then taste a blow from your old uncle!”

p.src: What a fine Monkey King! With one hand he seized her, while with the other he drew the cudgel from his ear. He gave it a shake, and it grew as thick as a rice bowl. The Rakshasa Woman wrenched herself free and raised her swords to meet him. The Pilgrim at once swung his cudgel and struck. Before Mount Emerald Cloud the two forgot all talk of kinship and reckoned only their enmity. What a fierce battle it was:

p.src: The Rakshasa Woman fought the Pilgrim until evening. Seeing that his cudgel was heavy and his technique flawless, she judged that she could not defeat him. She promptly took out the plantain-leaf fan, flourished it, and with one blast of a dark wind fanned the Pilgrim away until not a trace or shadow of him remained; there was no hope of his holding his ground. Victorious, the Rakshasa Woman returned to her cave.

p.src: The Great Sage drifted and tossed about, unable to sink to the ground on his left or find a foothold as he fell on his right. He was like withered leaves whirled by a gale, or fallen blossoms swept along by running water. He tumbled all night until dawn, when at last he landed on a mountain and clutched a crag with both hands. After steadying himself for a long while, he looked carefully and recognized the place as Mount Little Sumeru. The Great Sage heaved a long sigh and said, “What a formidable woman! How did she send old Monkey all the way here? I remember coming here years ago to ask the Bodhisattva Lingji to subdue the Yellow Wind Demon and save my master. Yellow Wind Ridge lies more than three thousand li due south of here, but now I have come back from the western road and am southeast of it; who knows how many tens of thousands of li I have been blown? I shall go down and ask the Bodhisattva Lingji for directions, so that I can return by the old road.”

p.src: While he was hesitating, he heard a bell ring loudly. He hurried down the slope and went straight to the monastery. The Daoist attendant at the gate recognized the Pilgrim’s appearance and went inside to report, “The hairy-faced Great Sage who came the year before last to ask the Bodhisattva to subdue the Yellow Wind Demon is here again.” Knowing it was Wukong, the Bodhisattva hastily descended from his precious throne to welcome him. After they entered and exchanged salutations, he asked, “Congratulations! Have you returned from fetching the scriptures?” Wukong replied, “We have not reached there yet. It is far too soon, far too soon.” Lingji said, “Since you have not yet reached Thunderclap Monastery, why have you turned back to this barren mountain?” The Pilgrim said, “Since you graciously subdued the Yellow Wind Demon for us last year, we have endured more hardships along the road than I could count. Now we have reached the Mountain of Flames and cannot advance. When I questioned the local people, they said that an Immortal of the Iron Fan possessed a plantain-leaf fan that could fan out the fire, so old Monkey went especially to seek her. It turned out that this immortal was the wife of the Bull Demon King and the mother of Red Boy. She said that because I had caused her son to become the Bodhisattva Guanyin’s attendant, she could no longer see him often. She hated me as an enemy, refused to lend me the fan, and fought with me. When she found my cudgel too heavy to withstand, she swept her fan at me and sent me drifting and floating all the way here, where at last I managed to land. That is why I have ventured to disturb your monastery and ask the way back. How many li is it from here to the Mountain of Flames?” Lingji laughed and said, “That woman is named the Rakshasa Woman and is also called Princess Iron Fan. Her plantain-leaf fan is a numinous treasure formed by Heaven and Earth behind the Kunlun Mountains when chaos was first divided. It is a leaf embodying the essence of the Great Yin, and therefore can extinguish fiery vapors. If it strikes a person, he must be blown eighty-four thousand li before the yin wind subsides. From my mountain to the Mountain of Flames is only a little over fifty thousand li. You stopped here only because, Great Sage, you possess the power to halt clouds; an ordinary mortal could never have stopped at all.” The Pilgrim said, “Formidable indeed, formidable indeed! But how is my master to cross that region?” Lingji said, “Set your mind at ease, Great Sage. Your coming here is also part of the destined affinity of the Tang Monk, and it is ordained that you should accomplish this feat.” The Pilgrim asked, “How am I to accomplish it?” Lingji replied, “Years ago, when I received the Tathagata’s command, he bestowed upon me a Wind-Stilling Pearl and a Flying Dragon Staff. The Flying Dragon Staff has already subdued the wind demon. The Wind-Stilling Pearl has never yet been used. I shall give it to you now, Great Sage, and I guarantee that wretch will be unable to fan you away. Then you may take her fan and fan out the fire. Will you not thereby accomplish this feat?” The Pilgrim bowed his head in salute and thanked him profusely. The Bodhisattva took a brocade pouch from his sleeve, removed the Wind-Stilling Pearl, placed it inside the Pilgrim’s collar, and sewed it securely in place with needle and thread. As he escorted the Pilgrim to the gate, he said, “I have no time to detain and entertain you. Go northwest from here, and you will reach the Rakshasa’s mountain domain.”

p.src: The Pilgrim took leave of Lingji, mounted his somersault cloud, and sped directly back to Mount Green Cloud, arriving in an instant. He struck the cave gate with his iron cudgel and cried, “Open up! Open up! Old Monkey has come to borrow the fan for a while!” The girl inside was so alarmed that she hurried to report, “Mistress, the fan-borrower has come again.” When the Rakshasa heard this, fear stirred in her heart. “That vile monkey truly has some skill. When my treasure fans someone, he must travel eighty-four thousand li before he can stop. How has he returned so soon after being blown away? This time I shall fan him two or three times in succession and make sure he can never find his way back.” She sprang up, dressed herself neatly, grasped her sword in both hands, and came out through the gate. “Sun the Pilgrim, are you unafraid of me, that you have come seeking death again?” The Pilgrim laughed. “Sister-in-law, do not be so stingy. You really must lend it to me for a while. Once the Tang Monk is safely across the mountain, I shall return it to you. I am an utterly sincere gentleman, not a petty man who borrows things and fails to return them.” The Rakshasa cursed him again. “You vile macaque! How utterly unreasonable and senseless you are! I have not yet avenged the theft of my son; how could your wish to borrow my fan ever be granted? Do not run away—take a stroke of my sword!” The Great Sage showed no fear at all and raised his iron cudgel to meet her blow. The two went back and forth for some five or seven rounds. The Rakshasa Woman’s arms weakened and could scarcely wield her sword, while Sun the Pilgrim was strong and skilled in combat. Seeing that matters were going badly, she took out her fan and swept it once at the Pilgrim, but he stood towering and unmoved. The Pilgrim put away his iron cudgel and said with a beaming smile, “This time is not like the last. Fan me however you please—if old Monkey moves even a fraction, I am no true man.” The Rakshasa fanned him twice more. Sure enough, he did not move. The Rakshasa panicked, hurriedly put away her treasure, turned back, and ran into the cave, shutting the gate tight behind her.

p.src: When the Pilgrim saw that she had closed the gate, he resorted to a trick. He opened his collar and held the Wind-Stilling Pearl in his mouth. With a shake of his body he changed into a tiny insect and crawled through a crack in her gate. He heard the Rakshasa cry, “I am thirsty! I am thirsty! Bring me tea quickly.” A girl attendant nearby promptly brought a pot of fragrant tea and poured a bowl brimful with a hiss, raising a thick froth upon it. The Pilgrim was delighted at the sight. With a buzz of his wings, he flew beneath the tea froth. The Rakshasa was desperately thirsty. She took the tea and swallowed it all in two or three draughts. The Pilgrim was now inside her belly. He resumed his true form and shouted fiercely, “Sister-in-law, lend me the fan for a while!” The Rakshasa turned pale with fright and cried, “You servants, did you close the front gate?” They all answered, “We closed it.” She said, “If the gate is closed, how can Sun the Pilgrim be shouting inside the house?” A girl replied, “He is shouting from inside your body.” The Rakshasa said, “Sun the Pilgrim, where are you performing your magic?” The Pilgrim replied, “Old Monkey has never practiced tricks in his life. These are all genuine methods and real abilities. I am already amusing myself inside my honored sister-in-law’s honored belly and have seen her lungs and liver. I know you are hungry and thirsty too, so first I shall give you a chamber pot to quench your thirst.” With that, he stamped his foot downward. The pain in the Rakshasa’s lower belly became unbearable. She sat down on the ground and cried out in agony. The Pilgrim said, “Sister-in-law, do not refuse my hospitality. I shall give you another snack to satisfy your hunger.” Then he thrust his head upward. The Rakshasa could not endure the pain in her heart. She rolled about on the ground, her face yellow and her lips white with agony, crying only, “Uncle Sun, spare my life!”

p.src: Only then did the Traveler cease his attack and say, “So now you acknowledge your uncle, do you? For Brother Bull’s sake, I shall spare your life for now. Quickly bring me the fan and let me use it.” The Rakshasi said, “Uncle, I have the fan, I have it! Come out and take it.” The Traveler said, “Bring the fan where I can see it, and then I shall come out.” The Rakshasi at once ordered a maid to fetch a plantain-leaf fan and hold it beside her. The Traveler climbed as far as her throat, saw the fan, and said, “Sister-in-law, since I have spared your life, I will not bore a hole through your ribs to come out, but shall leave by your mouth instead. Open your mouth three times.” The Rakshasi obediently opened her mouth. The Traveler changed back into a tiny insect, flew out first, and alighted on the plantain-leaf fan. Unaware of this, the Rakshasi opened her mouth three times in succession and called, “Come out, Uncle.” The Traveler resumed his true form, seized the fan, and cried, “Am I not right here? Many thanks for the loan, many thanks!” He strode off at once and went on his way. The underlings hurriedly opened the gate and let him out of the cave.

p.src: The Great Sage turned his cloud about and headed straight back east. In an instant he lowered it and stood beneath the red-brick wall. Seeing him, Eight Rules cried joyfully, “Master, Elder Brother is back! He is back!” Tripitaka immediately came out with the old master of the estate and Friar Sand to welcome him, and they all went inside together. Leaning the plantain-leaf fan against the wall, the Traveler asked, “Old sir, is this the fan?” The old man replied, “Yes, indeed! That is it!” The Tang Monk said delightedly, “Worthy disciple, you have rendered an immeasurable service. You must have endured great hardship to obtain this treasure.” The Traveler said, “The hardship itself is hardly worth mentioning. But who do you suppose that Immortal Iron Fan is? That wretch is none other than the wife of the Bull Demon King and the mother of Red Boy. Her name is the Rakshasi, and she is also called Princess Iron Fan. When I reached her cave and asked to borrow the fan, she brought up our old grievance and struck at me several times with her swords. I brandished my cudgel to frighten her, but she gave me one sweep of her fan and sent me drifting and tumbling all the way to Mount Little Sumeru. Fortunately, I met the Bodhisattva Lingji, who gave me a Wind-Fixing Pill and showed me the way back. I returned to Mount Green Cloud and met the Rakshasi again. She used the fan again, but when she could not move me with it, she retreated into her cave. Then old Monkey changed into a tiny insect and flew inside. The wretch happened to call for tea, so I hid beneath the froth, entered her belly, and set to work. Unable to endure the pain, she kept calling me uncle and begging for mercy, and willingly agreed to lend me the fan. So I spared her and brought the fan away. Once we have crossed the Mountain of Flames, I shall return it to her.” When Tripitaka heard this, his gratitude knew no bounds.

p.src: Master and disciples all took leave of the old man and continued westward. After traveling roughly forty li, they gradually found themselves assailed by a scorching heat. Friar Sand kept crying, “The soles of my feet are being seared!” Eight Rules added, “My trotters are painfully hot!” The horse went faster than usual, for the heat was unbearable and kept it from standing still, making it rush frantically onward. The Traveler said, “Master, please dismount for a while. Brothers, go no farther. Wait while I fan out the flames. After the wind and rain have passed and the ground has cooled somewhat, we shall cross the mountain.” The Traveler raised the fan and went straight to the edge of the flames. He swept it with all his might, but the fire on the mountain leaped roaring into the air; at the second sweep, it blazed a hundred times more fiercely; and at the third, the flames soared fully a thousand zhang high and began to scorch his body. The Traveler hastily retreated, but the hair on both his thighs had already been burned clean away. He ran straight back to the Tang Monk and cried, “Quickly, turn back! Turn back! The fire is coming! The fire is coming!”

p.src: The master scrambled onto his horse and, together with Eight Rules and Friar Sand, retreated more than twenty li eastward before stopping to rest. He asked, “Wukong, what happened?” The Traveler threw down the fan and said, “It is no good, no good at all! That wretch deceived me.” Hearing this, Tripitaka’s brows knitted with sorrow and his heart grew heavy with anguish. Tears streamed uncontrollably down his cheeks as he said, “What are we to do?” Eight Rules asked, “Brother, why did you call us back in such a hurry?” The Traveler replied, “When I swept the fan once, the flames roared up; at the second sweep, the fire grew fiercer still; and at the third, the flames leaped a thousand zhang into the air. Had I not run quickly, all my hair would have been burned away.” Eight Rules laughed and said, “You are always saying that thunder cannot hurt you and fire cannot harm you. Why are you afraid of fire now?” The Traveler replied, “You idiot, you understand nothing. On those occasions I guarded myself with due care, and so I came to no harm. Today I was intent only on fanning out the flames. I neither formed the fire-warding spell nor invoked the art that protects my body, and so the hair on both my thighs was burned away.” Friar Sand said, “With the fire raging like this, there is no road west. What are we to do?” Eight Rules said, “We need only choose a route where there is no fire.” Tripitaka asked, “In which direction is there no fire?” Eight Rules replied, “There is no fire to the east, south, or north.” He was asked again, “In which direction are the scriptures?” Eight Rules replied, “The scriptures are in the west.” Tripitaka said, “It is only to the place where the scriptures are that I wish to go.” Friar Sand said, “Where there are scriptures, there is fire; where there is no fire, there are no scriptures. We truly can neither advance nor retreat.”

Hearing this, Tripitaka’s brows knitted with sorrow and his heart grew heavy with anguish. Tears streamed uncontrollably down his cheeks as he said, “What are we to do?”

p.src: While master and disciples were still talking at random, they heard someone call, “Great Sage, do not distress yourself. Come and eat some vegetarian food, and then we can discuss the matter further.” The four pilgrims turned and saw an old man wearing a wind-billowed cloak and a crescent-shaped cap, carrying a dragon-headed staff in his hand and wearing iron-shafted boots. Behind him came a demon with a carved beak and fishlike cheeks, bearing a copper basin on its head. Inside were steamed cakes, millet gruel, and yellow-grain rice. Standing on the western road, the old man bowed and said, “I am the local god of the Mountain of Flames. Knowing that the Great Sage is protecting the holy monk but cannot proceed, I have specially come to offer you a vegetarian meal.” The Traveler said, “Eating is a small matter. When will these flames be extinguished so that my master may pass?” The local god replied, “To extinguish the flames, you must ask the Rakshasi to lend you her plantain-leaf fan.” The Traveler went to the roadside, picked up the fan, and said, “Is this not it? Why, then, do the flames burn more fiercely the more I fan them?” The local god examined it and said with a laugh, “This fan is false. She deceived you.” The Traveler asked, “How, then, can I obtain the true one?” The local god once more bent his back in a bow and said with a faint smile:
